subsection: 1. Changes in settlement patterns from rural to urban

notes.b: A settlement pattern is the way a population is spread across the land, in scattered rural homes and farms, villages, towns and cities. Over the last century Ireland's pattern shifted towards towns and cities, so a rising share of the population lives in urban areas while the countryside loses people.
points: Rural means countryside, farms and small villages; urban means towns and cities, where jobs, colleges and services are concentrated.
Urbanisation is the growth in the proportion of a country's population living in towns and cities. It is about a rising share, not just population growth.

Rural depopulation is the fall in the number of people living in the countryside, through migration to towns or abroad. Moving within Ireland is internal migration, while leaving the country is emigration; both can cause rural decline.
Rural depopulation is most marked in remote areas and where farm employment has fallen, because larger and mechanised farms need fewer workers.
Young adults are the group most likely to leave rural areas for education and first jobs, so many villages are left with an older population and fewer children.
Rural areas that lose population also lose local services such as post offices, Garda stations and schools, which makes rural life less attractive.

The movement is not one-way or uniform. Towns, commuter belts (the areas around cities where people live and travel to work) and some rural areas have grown while remote areas lost people, so the overall picture is mixed.
notes.tip: Do not mix up rural depopulation with emigration, and do not quote a census figure or percentage for the urban share, because it changes from census to census. Say 'a rising share'.

notes.h: Causes of movement to urban areas
notes.b: People move to towns and cities because that is where most opportunities are. Examiners want each reason explained, so give the reason and then say why it draws people.
points: Employment: towns and cities contain most of the jobs in manufacturing, services and office work. Larger, mechanised farms need fewer workers, so farm jobs fell, and the children of small farms could not all inherit land.
Education: third-level colleges and specialist schools and courses are concentrated in urban centres, so many young people move for college and do not return.
Services and infrastructure: hospitals, shops, public transport, entertainment, leisure facilities and fast broadband are more available, and better, in towns and cities.
Housing: towns offer a wider choice of rented and owned accommodation, including apartments for people without land.
Family and social ties: moving closer to friends, relatives, a partner or a partner's workplace draws many people into towns, and towns offer a bigger social life for young adults.
Young adults are the group most likely to leave, so the countryside is left with an older population and fewer children.
notes.tip: If asked for three or four reasons more people live in towns and cities, pick from jobs, education, services, housing, and family and friends. The marks go on the explanation, so each reason needs a 'because'.

notes.h: Effects of urbanisation on family life
notes.b: Living in a town or city changes how a family spends its time, money and support. There are gains and losses, and a good answer gives both.
points: Urban families have easier access to childcare, schools, health care, shops and entertainment, which can improve quality of life.
A wider choice of jobs means both parents can more easily find work, and there are more leisure facilities for the family to use.
Long commutes from suburbs to city workplaces reduce the time parents spend at home and add pressure to family routines.

High housing costs and high rents (because heavy demand meets limited housing) can delay marriage and the birth of children until young couples can afford a home, squeeze family budgets and cause overcrowding.
Urban neighbourhoods can face congestion, noise and air pollution, and crime and antisocial behaviour in some areas.
Families in cities are often farther from grandparents and extended family, so there is less daily childcare and practical help.
There is often less community spirit in cities, with neighbours who do not know each other, so families have less informal support.
notes.tip: Examiners reward effects in both directions. Do not say urban life is simply worse: tie each point to family life, not just geography, and compare with rural areas where asked.

notes.h: Effects of rural depopulation on family life
notes.b: When people leave the countryside, the families who stay feel it in their relationships and in the services they depend on. The loss feeds on itself, because fewer people mean fewer services, which makes the area less attractive to the next generation.
points: Older people living alone in rural areas can become isolated and lonely when younger family members move away, because fewer relatives are nearby for daily support.
Children in depopulated areas may attend smaller schools with fewer classmates, and grandparents are less available for childcare.
Teams and clubs struggle to field players, so children have fewer chances to take part in local activities.
Rural decline can cause whole family units to emigrate, weakening the local network of family and neighbourly support.

Withdrawal of services such as shops, post offices, banks, public transport, Garda stations and schools makes daily life harder for families who remain in the countryside. With fewer customers these services close, which makes the area less attractive to the next generation, a cycle of decline.
Family farms may have no heir, because the younger generation has moved away.
There are positives for those who stay: lower housing costs, a strong sense of community, lower crime and pollution, more space and safer play for children, and a slower pace of life.
notes.tip: Questions on movement from rural to urban areas ask for the impact on life in rural areas as well as in the city: cover older people, services and schools. Closures: say 'such as', with no numbers or place names.

notes.h: Why some rural areas have grown
notes.b: Rural depopulation is not the whole story, because some rural areas have gained people. Better connections and lower costs have made country living workable for families who would once have had to move to a town.
points: Better roads and transport let people live in the country and commute to work in towns and cities.
Cheaper housing and living costs make the countryside attractive to families, especially compared with high urban rents.
Lower crime and pollution make rural areas appealing places to raise children.
Improved local services, leisure and community facilities mean country life no longer means going without.
Broadband and working from home allow people to keep a job in a town or city while living in the countryside.
Rural resettlement and local-authority housing moves have brought families into some rural areas.
notes.tip: If asked why the number of people in some rural areas increased, give transport, cheaper housing and living costs, lower crime and pollution, improved services, remote working and resettlement, with a reason for each.

notes.h: Initiatives to keep population in rural areas
notes.b: Governments and state agencies have used job creation and infrastructure to slow rural depopulation. People stay where they can earn a living and where services remain, so most initiatives aim to create local jobs or make country living practical.
points: Redeployment (decentralisation) of government departments and state agencies to rural and regional towns creates public-sector jobs outside the cities and Dublin.
Rural resettlement schemes help families, including city families, move to and settle in the countryside, which helps keep rural communities viable and schools and services open.
IDA Ireland is the agency responsible for attracting investment from overseas companies. It encourages foreign firms to locate in regional towns as well as the cities, creating jobs.
Enterprise Ireland helps Irish firms to start, grow and export, including firms outside Dublin, so jobs are created locally.

Local Enterprise Offices, one in each local authority area, give advice, mentoring, training and small grants to micro and small businesses. Local people can then create their own jobs, for example in cottage industries, craft and food businesses and tourism.
Údarás na Gaeltachta is the regional authority responsible for the economic, social and cultural development of the Gaeltacht areas, encouraging enterprise and jobs there.
LEADER is the EU-funded rural development programme that supports community-led local projects such as village renewal, tourism and enterprise.

Investment in roads, public transport, electricity and telecommunications, especially broadband (the National Broadband Plan, which aims to bring high-speed broadband to areas the market did not serve), makes rural living and remote or hybrid working practical, and remote-working hubs in towns support this.
Community employment and training programmes, for example in childcare, horticulture and caring, give rural people skills and work experience.
notes.tip: When asked to name and give details of one initiative, name it (about 4 marks), then give two details of what it does and how it keeps people or jobs in the area. Do not give dates, job totals or town names.

notes.h: Comparing family life then and now
notes.b: A good way to understand settlement change is to compare family life a hundred years ago with today, and to ask someone who lived through it.
points: Compare who lived on the land, the size of families, school attendance and leisure then and now.
Interview an older relative or community member about when people left the area, why they left, and what changed.

keyTerms.definition: The growth in the proportion of a country's population living in towns and cities.
The decline in the number of people living in the countryside, usually through migration to towns or abroad.
The way people are spread across the landscape, in dispersed rural homes, villages, towns and cities.
The relocation of government departments or agencies from the capital to regional locations.
Travelling regularly between home and work, often over a long distance.
The growth of residential areas on the edge of cities, from which residents travel daily to work in the city.
A scheme that helps people settle in rural areas in order to slow the loss of rural population.
Low-density development spreading outward from a city into surrounding countryside.

factCards.term: Four reasons people move from rural to urban areas
factCards.definition: Employment, education, services and infrastructure, and a wider choice of housing.

factCards.term: Three problems facing older people left in rural villages
factCards.definition: Isolation, the closure of local services, and fewer relatives nearby to give daily support.

factCards.term: Four effects of urbanisation on family life
factCards.definition: Greater distance from extended family, long commutes, high housing costs, and urban congestion or pollution.

factCards.term: Three kinds of state support for rural enterprise
factCards.definition: Overseas investment attraction through IDA Ireland, growth support for Irish firms through Enterprise Ireland, and local enterprise advice and grants for small businesses.

questions.prompt: State two reasons why many people in Ireland have moved from rural areas to urban areas in recent decades.
questions.model: Employment: most jobs are located in towns and cities. Services: better access to third-level education, hospitals, shops and public transport. Housing: a wider choice of housing and rental accommodation is available in towns.

questions.prompt: Explain how the growth of towns and cities and the decline of rural populations have affected the daily lives and support networks of Irish families. Refer to at least one state initiative that aims to keep people in rural areas.
questions.model: Urban growth: families are often far from grandparents and relatives, so informal childcare and practical help are reduced. Commuting from suburbs lengthens the working day and reduces family time. Housing costs in cities can delay family formation. Urban areas offer better access to childcare, health and education services, but may suffer congestion, pollution and some crime and antisocial behaviour. Rural decline: older people living alone can become isolated when younger relatives emigrate or move to cities. Local services such as shops, post offices and schools close, making daily family life harder. Children may attend smaller schools with fewer peers. Initiative: redeployment of government departments and state agencies to rural towns creates public-sector jobs; IDA Ireland and Enterprise Ireland support investment and firms outside the cities; improved roads and broadband allow remote working.
